claims.text: The initial alloy is an as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy containing dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The initial alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
Microcracking at internal lamellar boundaries causes the limited room-temperature ductility.
Approximately 0.2–0.5 at% boron should be added to the alloy.
The boron-containing alloy should be solution annealed at approximately 1100 °C and rapidly cooled.
Approximately 1100 °C lies within the alloy's single-phase region.
Boron addition followed by solution annealing and quenching will produce boron segregation at lamellar interphase boundaries.
Segregated boron modifies chemical bonding and increases cohesion at lamellar interfaces.
Greater lamellar-interface cohesion decreases crack initiation at the boundaries.
Greater lamellar-interface cohesion decreases crack propagation from the boundaries.
Reduced boundary cracking promotes stable plastic deformation in the dual-phase structure.
The boron-doped and solution-annealed alloy will have higher room-temperature tensile elongation than the unmodified baseline.
The boron-doped and solution-annealed alloy will maintain or modestly increase yield strength relative to the unmodified baseline.
The as-cast baseline typically exhibits only a few percent tensile elongation.
Excess boron can form brittle borides.
Brittle boride formation would negate the proposed ductility improvement.
Insufficient solution treatment could negate the proposed ductility improvement.

contradictions.description: The stated outcome is relative to an as-cast baseline, but the falsification experiment solution-anneals both the doped and undoped samples. The experimental control therefore does not match the stated as-cast baseline and cannot isolate the full intervention relative to that baseline.
